title: Chapter 85: Core of the Truehearted 7
content:
Chapter 85

Core of the Truehearted 7

Before crossing the threshold of Lotus Pier, Wei Wuxian took a long, measured breath to steady his nerves. But once he actually stepped inside, the grand swell of emotion he’d braced for never came.

Maybe it was because so much of the place had been completely rebuilt. The training grounds had doubled in size, sprawling out beneath rows of sleek new pavilions whose upturned eaves interlocked in crisp, imposing layers. It was grander than it used to be, undoubtedly more majestic, but compared to the Lotus Pier burned into his memory, it was almost unrecognizable.

A hollow ache settled in Wei Wuxian’s chest. He couldn't tell if the old, weathered halls of his youth were merely hidden behind these lavish new facades, or if they’d been torn down altogether.

They really had been so very old, after all.

Across the training grounds, disciples from the various clans broke into neat squares, dropping cross-legged to meditate and nurse their battered spiritual cores. After nearly a full day and night of non-stop madness, everyone was running on fumes; they desperately needed a breather. Meanwhile, Jiang Cheng led the clan leaders and prominent figures inside toward the main hall—the Sword Testing Hall—to hash out the day's fallout. Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji fell in step right behind them. A few people clearly found their presence inappropriate, but nobody had the nerve to say it out loud.

They had barely cleared the threshold and hadn't even taken their seats when a man dressed as a guest retainer hurried forward. "Sect Leader."

He leaned in, murmuring a few hushed sentences into Jiang Cheng’s ear. Jiang Cheng’s brow instantly pinched. "Turn them away. Whatever it is can wait until later. Can’t you see what kind of situation we’re dealing with right now?"

"I tried telling them that," the retainer pressed, "but the two women insisted... they’re here specifically because of today’s incident."

"Who are they?" Jiang Cheng demanded. "Which sect do they cultivate for?"

"Neither. They aren't cultivators at all," the retainer answered. "I checked thoroughly—they’re ordinary women with zero spiritual energy. They both arrived today, bringing along a haul of exceptionally rare medicinal herbs. They wouldn't say which clan head sent them, only that they had critical news for you, Sect Leader. What they claim to know sounds far too serious to brush off, so I didn't dare turn them away. I put them up in the guest quarters for now, and the herbs haven't been moved into the vaults yet. I already had them inspected—no curses or foul play detected."

A pair of commoners with no spiritual cultivation and no clan backing demanding an audience with the leader of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect—while refusing to give their names—should have been dismissed on the spot. But they had arrived bearing a mountain of priceless medicine. Even looking past the sheer value of the gift, the sheer bizarre timing of it was impossible to ignore.

Jiang Cheng turned to the room. "Everyone, please, make yourselves comfortable. Forgive me for a moment; I'll be right back."

A chorus of polite murmurs followed him: "Take your time, Sect Leader Jiang."

Jiang Cheng, however, did not come right back. Abandoning a hall full of guests was bad manners under normal circumstances, let alone during a high-stakes crisis when dozens of clan heads were waiting to hold council. As the better part of an hour dragged on without a sign of him, the room grew thick with restless murmurs and souring tempers.

Just as the grumbling reached a boil, Jiang Cheng finally strode back in. The neutral composure he’d left with was gone, replaced by a grim, razor-sharp scowl. He walked with urgent, clipped strides, trailing two women behind him—evidently the mysterious guests.

The room had braced for something extraordinary; surely commoners bearing lavish gifts must carry themselves with rare grace. Instead, both women were well past their prime, lines of age etched deep around their eyes and mouths. One kept her head ducked low, shaking like a cornered rabbit. The other reeked unmistakably of cheap brothels, her face slashed with five or six jagged, faded scars that turned her features into a grotesque mask.

It was an outright stomach-churning sight. Disappointment curdled into baffled whispers as the cultivators traded bewildered glances, wondering why on earth Jiang Cheng had dragged two such wretched women into the sacred Sword Testing Hall—and why he was gesturing for them to stand dead-center in the room.

Jiang Cheng’s face was dark as a thundercloud. Turning to the trembling pair as they took their seats, he said, "Speak. Right here."

Sect Leader Yao frowned. "Sect Leader Jiang, what is the meaning of this?"

"The matter is so appalling that I refused to jump to conclusions," Jiang Cheng said evenly. "I interrogated them thoroughly myself, which is why I was delayed. Quiet down, all of you, and hear what they have to say." He glanced at the women. "Which of you goes first?"

The two traded a hesitant look. The scarred, worldly woman had the thicker skin; she pushed herself up from her chair. "I'll go!"

Offering a lazy, haphazard curtsy, she began, "What I have to share happened about eleven years ago."

Hearing Jiang Cheng’s deadly serious tone, the room knew this couldn't be trivial gossip, and minds raced to recall whatever scandals had rocked the world eleven years back.

"My name is Sisi," she stated plainly. "I used to work the skin trade. Made quite a name for myself in my younger days, too. About a decade ago, I found a wealthy merchant who wanted to take me in as a concubine. Who would've guessed his wife was a vicious piece of work? She hired a pack of thugs with blades to carve up my face, and that was that. Ruined."

She spoke of her sordid past without a drop of shame or hesitation, making the female cultivators shield their mouths with their sleeves while the men pinched their brows in disgust.

Sisi carried on, entirely unfazed: "Once my face was butchered like this, life took a sharp turn. Nobody would look at me, let alone pay for my time. The brothel kicked me straight out the door. I didn't know how to do anything else, and with no customers willing to hire me, I ended up shacking up with some older working girls down in the alleys. Their clients weren't picky. Whenever work came in, they’d throw a scrap my way; wrap a veil over my ugly mug, and I could still scrape together a living."

By this point, several cultivators were visibly squirming, their sneering disgust laid bare. Why the hell was Jiang Cheng forcing them to sit through the vulgar whining of a washed-up whore? The older clan leaders, however, held their tongues, waiting for the other shoe to drop.

Sure enough, she cut straight to the point.

"Then, out of nowhere, a massive job landed in our alley. Someone put in an order for over twenty of us, complete with private carriages to haul us out. The pay was negotiated upfront, and my older sisters were thrilled to death on the ride over. But my gut told me something was rotten. Let’s call a spade a spade—we were either dried-up old crones or mangled freaks like me. Paying that kind of fortune upfront? There’s no such thing as a free lunch in this world. On top of that, the client was skulking around in the shadows, packing us into covered carriages under the dead of night so nobody in the neighborhood saw a thing. Nothing about it smelled right."

The room had to concede she had a point; disgust gave way to hooked curiosity.

"When the carriages finally stopped, we were ushered into an inner courtyard," Sisi continued. "None of us had ever laid eyes on buildings so massive, so grand, so dripping in gold. It nearly blinded us; we barely dared to breathe. A young lad was leaning against the entrance tossing a dagger around. The second he spotted us, he waved us inside and barred the door.

"Inside that cavernous room, there were only two people. Lying under a lavish silk quilt on an enormous bed was a man—looked to be in his late thirties or early forties, sick as a dog and half-dead. When we walked in, the only part of him that could even move was his eyes."

"Ah!"

A sharp gasp cut through the hall as someone put the pieces together. "Eleven years ago?! That’s... that’s—!"

"We’d already been drilled on what to do," Sisi said, ignoring the outburst. "We were supposed to take turns pulling out every trick in our repertoire to work the man in that bed. Non-stop. I’d figured the client was some virile brute; turns out he was a wheezing invalid. A man in that state couldn't take that kind of punishment! A few rounds and he’d be a corpse. What kind of lust-crazed degenerate signs his own death warrant like that? And with that kind of money, it wasn't like they couldn't afford fresh, pretty young girls. Why specifically order a batch of old, ugly hags?

"I was crawling onto him, turning it over in my head, when a young man suddenly chuckled. It scared the living daylights out of me—only then did I notice a privacy screen beside the bed, and someone was sitting right behind it!"

The entire room held its collective breath.

"He’d been sitting behind that screen the whole damn time," Sisi said, her voice dropping. "The moment he laughed, the man on the bed suddenly thrashed, shoving me off and tumbling onto the floorboards. The man behind the screen just laughed harder. Between chuckles, he said: 'Father, I’ve brought you your favorite kind of women. Plenty of them, too. Aren't you pleased?'"

The words came from a broken courtesan, but an icy dread crawled down every spine in the hall, conjuring the exact same smiling face in every mind.

Jin Guangyao!

And the dying man on that bed could only be Jin Guangshan!

Jin Guangshan’s death had always been an open secret among the sects. The man had spent his life indulging an appetite so lecherous it bordered on vile, scattering bastards and scandals across every province. His demise had matched his lifestyle: the venerable leader of the Lanling Jin Sect, refusing to curb his carnal appetites even as his health failed, ultimately dropping dead in the saddle. It was wildly humiliating to speak of. Madame Jin, already wasting away with grief over the deaths of her only son and daughter-in-law, believed her husband had literally whored himself into an early grave; the sheer fury had made her sick, and she followed him to the yellow springs shortly after. Lanling Jin had moved mountains to suppress the whispers, but the other clans all knew. Outwardly they offered solemn condolences, but behind closed doors, everyone agreed it was the exact pathetic end a dog like him deserved.

Yet the reality laid bare before them now was something infinitely more twisted, infinitely more depraved. A ripple of sharp, horrified gasps echoed across the hall.

"That middle-aged man tried to scream, tried to fight back, but he was completely paralyzed," Sisi pressed on. "Then that lad who brought us in kicked the door open again, giggling like a maniac. He dragged the man back onto the mattress, grabbed a length of rope, stepped straight on his skull to pin him down, and trussed him up like a pig. Then he looked at us and said: 'Keep going. Even if he dies, do not stop.'

"None of us had ever witnessed madness like that! We were terrified out of our wits, but we didn't dare disobey, so we kept at it. By the eleventh or twelfth girl, someone screamed—he’d actually died. I leaned in to check, and sure enough, he’d stopped breathing. But the voice behind the screen just said: 'Didn't you hear me? Even if he's dead, don't you dare stop.'"

Sect Leader Ouyang couldn't stomach it any longer. "Whatever else he was, Jin Guangshan was his biological father! If this is true... this is... this is monstrous!"

"The second that man stopped breathing, I knew we were finished," Sisi said, her voice shaking faintly. "There was no way they’d let witnesses walk. Sure enough, once it was over, every single one of my twenty-odd sisters was slaughtered. Not a soul spared..."

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. "Then why were you the only one left alive?"

"I don't know!" Sisi blurted out. "I fell to my knees, weeping and begging for my life, swearing I didn't want a single copper of their money and that my lips were sealed forever. And for some reason, they actually spared me. They dragged me off to some compound and locked me in a room for eleven years. It was only recently that someone broke in, saved me, and helped me escape."

"Who saved you?" Wei Wuxian asked.

"I don't know," she said, shaking her head. "I never saw my benefactor’s face. But once that noble gentleman heard my story, he refused to let a hypocritical, depraved butcher keep pulling the wool over the world's eyes. He said that even if that man holds the heavens in the palm of his hand today, every foul deed must be dragged into the light—to give his victims justice, and let my twenty-odd sisters finally rest in peace."
